title: SELECT: Reading Data
summary: SELECT chooses which columns to show from a table. FROM tells SQL which table to read.
introduction: SELECT chooses which columns to show from a table. FROM tells SQL which table to read. Start by reading every column, then ask for only the two you need. Give an answer column a clear name.
learningObjectives: Select specific columns instead of every column
Compute new values with arithmetic expressions

blocks.text: `SELECT` lists what you want in the result and `FROM` names the table. Column names are separated by commas, and the order in which you list them is the order of the result columns.

blocks.content:
name              | country
------------------+------------
Ada Lovelace      | UK
Grace Hopper      | US
Linus Torvalds    | Finland
Margaret Hamilton | US
Guido van Rossum  | Netherlands

blocks.text: `SELECT *` is shorthand for every column in the table's defined order. It is convenient while exploring, but in application code it is better to name the columns you need: the result stays stable when someone adds a column later, and the database transfers less data.

Anything that produces a value can be a result column: a column, a number, an arithmetic expression, a function call. The expression is evaluated for every row. Here `ROUND(price * 1.2, 2)` adds 20% tax and rounds to two decimals:

blocks.code:
SELECT name, price, ROUND(price * 1.2, 2) AS price_with_tax
FROM products;

blocks.content:
name                | price | price_with_tax
--------------------+-------+---------------
Notebook            | 4.5   | 5.4
Mouse pad           | 8.99  | 10.79
USB cable           | 12    | 14.4
Mechanical keyboard | 89    | 106.8
Monitor stand       | 39.5  | 47.4
Sticky notes        | 2.75  | 3.3

blocks.text: Notice that `4.50` is shown as `4.5` and `12.00` as `12`: SQLite stores the prices as floating-point `REAL` values, and the playground prints such numbers without trailing zeros (the `sqlite3` command-line shell would print `12.0`). Databases with a `DECIMAL(10,2)` type keep the two decimals; the [data types lesson](/tutorials/sql/create-table) comes back to this.

Without an alias, a calculated column is named after its expression, which is awkward to read and to reference from code. `AS` gives the column a name of your choice. The keyword is optional in most databases (`price * 1.2 tax` also works) but writing it makes the intent obvious. A name containing spaces or punctuation must be wrapped in double quotes:

blocks.content:
Product name | Price (EUR)
-------------+------------
Notebook     | 4.5
Mouse pad    | 8.99

blocks.text: Aliases can also shorten table names (`FROM customers AS c`), which becomes essential when joining tables in [JOINs](/tutorials/sql/joins).

Two customers live in the US, so selecting `country` returns `US` twice. `SELECT DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result. With several columns, DISTINCT keeps each distinct *combination* of values.
The rows come back in the order in which the database happened to find them; nothing guarantees it. The next lesson introduces `ORDER BY`, the only way to ask for a specific order.

A SELECT does not need a FROM clause: it can evaluate expressions directly, which is handy for testing a function or a calculation. SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server all accept this; Oracle traditionally requires `FROM DUAL`.

blocks.title: Double quotes are for names, single quotes for text
blocks.text: In standard SQL `'SQL'` is a text value and `"SQL"` is an identifier (a column or table name). SQLite tolerates `"SQL"` as a string when no such column exists, but PostgreSQL reports *column "SQL" does not exist*. Use single quotes for values and double quotes only for names that need them, such as the aliases with spaces above.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: In the runner, add a column `doubled` that holds twice the price, then write a second query that lists each category once with `DISTINCT`.

blocks.title: Try it yourself

questions.question: What does `SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products` return?
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows, so each of the three category names appears exactly once.
options: The first product of each category

questions.question: `SELECT *` is the recommended way to read data in application code because it always returns every column.
questions.explanation: Returning every column is exactly the problem: the result changes whenever the table changes and more data is transferred than needed. Name the columns you use.

seo.title: SQL SELECT – Columns, Expressions, Aliases, DISTINCT
seo.description: Learn the SQL SELECT statement: choose columns, compute values with expressions, rename results with AS and remove duplicate rows with DISTINCT.
